title: The crossing to Kyushu and the coming of rice, c. 1000–300 BC
summary: Wet-rice farming appears first in northern Kyushu, with tools and pottery of Korean types, and the hunter-gatherer Jōmon give way to the Yayoi. Some scholars see an influx of farmers from the continent; others credit the farming itself for much of the rise in numbers. The start is disputed: radiocarbon dates could push it back to 1000–800 BC against the usual 300 BC.

legs.source: Yayoi period (Wikipedia): farming methods, tools and some pottery traits came from Korea; the earliest evidence is in northern Kyushu
legs.doubt: When it began, and whether it was a movement of people or of farming, is argued: the radiocarbon dates that would take it back to 1000–800 BC are highly controversial, and some scholars say migration alone cannot explain the rise in numbers.
legs.note: A second reading brings irrigated rice from the Yangtze region by way of the Ryukyu islands; it is not drawn.

events.label: Itazuke, northern Kyushu
events.text: Itazuke, or Nabatake nearby, is named among the earliest sites of wet-rice farming; the article says it is still debated. The usual date for the Yayoi is about 300 BC to AD 300.
